decisions.parentContext: Fabric notes, delta pack, architecture section. The surrounding note distinguishes storage surfaces from processing stages.
decisions.reading: The note separates four things that are usually conflated: raw Files, Delta Tables, OneLake as the tenant-wide storage foundation, and a lakehouse as one Fabric item that uses OneLake. Bronze/silver/gold are processing stages, not separate storage products. Spark, the SQL analytics endpoint, storage APIs, REST management and Power BI are different consumption surfaces.
decisions.evidenceQuote: OneLake is the tenant-wide storage foundation, built on ADLS technology.

relationHints.claim: A lakehouse is a Fabric item that uses OneLake, so understanding what a lakehouse is depends on understanding the storage foundation it sits on.
relationHints.conditions: Holds for the OneLake-backed lakehouse described in the note; does not claim OneLake and lakehouse are the same object.

decisions.rationale: The matcher ranked OneLake secondary behind lakehouse. The passage defines OneLake explicitly and the review goal targets OneLake, so demoting it would misrepresent the unit.

decisions.parentContext: Fabric notes, delta pack, shortcut section. Follows the architecture note that defines OneLake and lakehouse.
decisions.reading: A shortcut is a reference to existing files or tables rather than an independently managed copy. Internal shortcuts can expose Files and Delta Tables; external sources include ADLS, S3, GCS, Dataverse and supported Iceberg integrations. Workspace caching reduces repeat remote reads, with a documented 1-28 day inactivity retention and a 1 GB file exclusion.
decisions.evidenceQuote: A plain shortcut references existing files or tables across workspaces or supported external systems
decisions.rationale: The matcher's primary candidate is the actual subject. The numeric caching limits are version-sensitive and are carried as conditions rather than as timeless facts.
unresolved: Caching retention (1-28 days) and the 1 GB exclusion must be re-verified against current Microsoft documentation before publication.

decisions.parentContext: Opening section of the SQL reference module: a learning map and decision framework, not a technique lesson.
decisions.reading: The framework asks what one output row should represent before choosing a technique. Branches map to JOIN, EXISTS, GROUP BY, window functions, set operations and CTEs. Grain and population are the entry questions; the technique is downstream.
decisions.evidenceQuote: Choose a SQL technique from the required population and output grain.

relationHints.claim: Choosing a set operation changes which rows survive, so the choice depends on the intended output grain.
relationHints.conditions: Applies when the set operation is selected to change the row population rather than only to concatenate disjoint results.

decisions.rationale: Set operations appeared as a co-primary candidate but the unit mentions it as one branch of a decision tree. Population was only secondary even though the opening sentence names it alongside grain.
unresolved: The decision flowchart lost its edge labels during extraction; only the branch targets survived, so the exact routing between questions cannot be reconstructed from the ledger alone.

decisions.parentContext: Statistics source, section 11, in a sequence that introduces population/sample before the sampling distribution and the central limit theorem.
decisions.reading: If many sufficiently sized samples are drawn from a population and each sample mean is computed, the distribution of those means approaches a normal distribution under suitable conditions, even when the population is not normal. The mean of that sampling distribution equals the population mean.
decisions.evidenceQuote: إذا أخذنا عددًا كبيرًا من العينات ذات الحجم المناسب من Population

relationHints.claim: The central limit theorem is a statement about the sampling distribution of the mean, so that distribution must be understood first.
relationHints.conditions: Under suitable conditions on sample size and dependence; the theorem does not make the raw population normal.

decisions.rationale: The matcher already had the right primary and the relation is supported verbatim. The secondary sampling-distribution candidate is promoted because the theorem is defined in terms of it.
unresolved: The extracted text references the mean-equality formula but the formula body is not present in the ledger.

decisions.parentContext: Statistics source, section 13, after the sampling distribution and before confidence intervals.
decisions.reading: Standard error is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic. For a sample mean it shrinks as sample size grows, which is why the estimate of the population mean becomes more stable. The section explicitly contrasts SD (spread of individual values) with SE (variation of the sample statistic between samples).
decisions.evidenceQuote: Standard Error هو Standard Deviation الخاص بـ Sampling Distribution للـ Statistic.

relationHints.claim: Standard error is defined as the standard deviation of the sampling distribution, so the sampling distribution is the prior idea.
relationHints.conditions: Applies to the sampling distribution of the statistic in question, not only the mean.

decisions.rationale: Direct definitional support. The SD/SE contrast is a misconception guard, not a second concept.
unresolved: The sigma/sqrt(n) and s/sqrt(n) formulas are referenced but absent from the extracted text.

decisions.parentContext: Statistics source, section 14, after standard error and before hypothesis testing.
decisions.reading: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for a population parameter from a sample and a specified method. The section rejects the claim that a computed 95% interval has a 95% probability of containing a fixed parameter, and gives the frequentist repeated-sampling interpretation. Width increases with confidence level and standard error and decreases with sample size.
decisions.evidenceQuote: فنحن لا نقول بدقة إن هناك

relationHints.claim: Interval width is driven by standard error, so the interval cannot be interpreted without it.
relationHints.conditions: For the normal-approximation and t-based intervals described in the section.

decisions.rationale: The matcher proposed concept:fabric:pipeline-parameter because the word parameter appears. Here parameter means a population parameter, so the fabric candidate is a lexical false positive and was removed.
unresolved: The general and standard interval formulas are referenced but not extracted.

decisions.parentContext: Statistics source, section 15, the hypothesis-testing section that closes the current slice.
decisions.reading: Hypothesis testing is a set of methods for comparing populations or evaluating a claim about a population. It starts from a null hypothesis of no difference or no effect to limit bias. The alternative can be two-sided or one-sided, and that choice defines what counts as more extreme when the p-value is computed.
decisions.evidenceQuote: نبدأ عادةً بافتراض عدم وجود فرق أو تأثير، لتقليل التحيز.

relationHints.claim: A p-value is the probability of results at least as extreme under the null, computed from the null sampling distribution.
relationHints.conditions: Requires a specified test statistic and a valid null model.

decisions.rationale: The matcher proposed concept:sql:population from the word population. In this unit population is the statistical population, not the query row population, so the SQL candidate was removed and p-value was added from the section's own definition.
unresolved: Only 15.1 and 15.2 are present in the extracted slice; the p-value and decision-rule subsections are outside the captured text.

decisions.parentContext: Visualization core chart types, section 6, inside the chart-by-chart reference. The page is a visualization lesson but the claim it makes is statistical.
decisions.reading: A scatter plot is for two continuous variables when the goal is to understand their relationship. The reader inspects direction, strength, form, outliers, clusters and changing variance. Correlation quantifies the strength and direction of a linear association only, and the Datasaurus examples show that very different shapes can share a correlation.
decisions.evidenceQuote: Positive correlation: larger X tends to accompany larger Y.

relationHints.claim: Reading a relationship plot depends on understanding what correlation does and does not summarize.
relationHints.conditions: For linear association; the unit itself warns that correlation is not a complete description of arbitrary relationships.

decisions.rationale: Correlation was only a secondary candidate because the page lives in the visualization domain. The unit's central caution is statistical, and this is a genuine cross-domain reuse of a canonical concept rather than a shared term.
unresolved: The page references figure content that was not visually reviewed.
Emphasis markers were stripped during extraction and adjacent words were joined (a linear association became alinearassociation), so exact quoting requires care.
